propositions.text: Whether self-induced intoxication is a defence to a charge of arson under s. 434 of the Criminal Code.
propositions.quote: This case requires the Court to determine whether self-induced intoxication is a defence to a charge of arson under s. 434 of the Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46 .

propositions.text: Mr. Tatton, the respondent, was charged after a fire destroyed his ex-girlfriend’s home, which began after he left oil on the stove while intoxicated.
propositions.quote: The charge against the respondent, Mr. Tatton, arose out of a fire that destroyed the contents of his ex-girlfriend’s home. The fire began after Mr. Tatton, in a highly intoxicated state, placed a pan with oil on the stove, set the burner to “high”, and left the house to get a coffee at a nearby Tim Hortons. When he returned approximately 20 minutes later, the house was on fire.

paragraphs.summary: The court must decide if self-induced intoxication is a defence to arson; Mr. Tatton was charged after causing a fire while intoxicated.

propositions.text: At trial, Mr. Tatton relied on accident due to drunkenness to rebut intent for arson.
propositions.quote: At trial, Mr. Tatton sought to rely on the defence of accident based on his drunkenness to rebut the intent required for the offence of arson.

propositions.text: The trial judge and a majority of the Court of Appeal agreed he could do so.
propositions.quote: The trial judge found that he could do so, and a majority of the Court of Appeal agreed.

propositions.text: The trial judge and majority of the Court of Appeal erred; intoxication short of automatism is not a defence to arson under s. 434.
propositions.quote: For reasons that follow, I am respectfully of the view that the trial judge and the majority of the Court of Appeal erred. Intoxication short of automatism is not a defence to a charge of arson under s. 434 of the Criminal Code .

paragraphs.summary: Mr. Tatton used drunkenness to claim accident at trial; lower courts accepted this, but the Supreme Court finds this was an error.

propositions.text: In September 2010, Mr. Tatton lived in a guest room at his ex-girlfriend Ms. Spencer’s home, hoping for reconciliation.
propositions.quote: In September 2010, Mr. Tatton was living in a guest room at a home owned by his ex-girlfriend, Ms. Spencer. He and Ms. Spencer had broken off their relationship, but Mr. Tatton remained hopeful that they would reconcile.

paragraphs.summary: Mr. Tatton lived in his ex-girlfriend's home, hoping to reconcile after their breakup.

propositions.text: Mr. Tatton was an alcoholic with a history of binge drinking, blackouts, and starting fires while intoxicated.
propositions.quote: Mr. Tatton was an alcoholic. He had a tendency to binge drink. There was evidence that in the past he had come home drunk, started to cook food, and then passed out, only to awake to a house filled with smoke. His history with alcoholism included periods of blackouts. He would sometimes have no recollection of events that had transpired while he was under the influence of alcohol.

paragraphs.summary: Mr. Tatton had a history of alcoholism, blackouts, and starting fires while drunk.

propositions.text: On September 24, 2010, Ms. Spencer left to visit friends; Mr. Tatton became upset, drank heavily, and left agitated messages referencing fire.
propositions.quote: On September 24, 2010, Ms. Spencer went to Kingston to visit friends. Mr. Tatton was not happy about this and became jealous and upset. He drank heavily throughout the day and evening, consuming approximately 52 ounces of alcohol. Over the course of the evening, he left Ms. Spencer a series of agitated voice messages on her cell phone, two of which referred to her home being on fire. Eventually, Mr. Tatton passed out.

paragraphs.summary: Mr. Tatton became upset, drank heavily, and left messages referencing fire after Ms. Spencer left to visit friends.

propositions.text: After waking, Mr. Tatton put oil on the stove, left for coffee, and returned to find the house on fire; he called 911 and later apologized.
propositions.quote: When Mr. Tatton awoke, he decided to cook some bacon. He put some vegetable oil in a pan on the stove and set the temperature to “high”. He then drove to a nearby Tim Hortons to get a coffee. When he returned 15-20 minutes later, the house was on fire. Mr. Tatton called 911 from a neighbouring house. The firefighters were able to save the home, but not its contents. The next day, Mr. Tatton left Ms. Spencer a message apologizing for the incident and stating that it was an accident.

paragraphs.summary: Mr. Tatton left oil on the stove, left for coffee, returned to a fire, called 911, and later apologized, calling it an accident.

propositions.text: The fire investigator found the fire started from the oil on the stove; Mr. Tatton was charged with arson under s. 434.
propositions.quote: The fire investigator determined that the source of the fire was the vegetable oil on the stove. Mr. Tatton was arrested and charged with arson contrary to s. 434 of the Criminal Code .

propositions.text: Section 434 criminalizes intentionally or recklessly causing damage by fire or explosion to property not wholly owned by the person.
propositions.quote: 434. Every person who intentionally or recklessly causes damage by fire or explosion to property that is not wholly owned by that person is guilty of an indictable offence and liable to imprisonment for a term not exceeding fourteen years.

paragraphs.summary: The fire started from oil on the stove; Mr. Tatton was charged under s. 434, which covers intentional or reckless fire damage to others' property.

propositions.text: At trial, Mr. Tatton claimed the fire was accidental, believing he set the stove to 'low' and lacking intent or foresight of consequences.
propositions.quote: At trial, Mr. Tatton claimed that the fire was an accident. When he put the oil on the stove, he thought he had set the temperature at “low”. He did not intend or foresee the consequences that resulted from his turning the stove on and leaving it unattended.

propositions.text: A central trial question was whether Mr. Tatton had the requisite intent for arson and if intoxication could be considered in assessing intent.
propositions.quote: A central question at trial was whether Mr. Tatton had the requisite intent to commit the offence of arson under s. 434 , and more particularly whether the court could take his state of intoxication into account in making its assessment.

paragraphs.summary: Mr. Tatton claimed accident, believing he set the stove to 'low'; the trial focused on his intent and whether intoxication was relevant.

propositions.text: The trial judge found s. 434 to be a specific intent offence, allowing Mr. Tatton to rely on intoxication as a defence.
propositions.quote: The trial judge determined that s. 434 was a specific intent offence, meaning that Mr. Tatton could rely on self-induced intoxication as a defence.

propositions.text: The trial judge acquitted Mr. Tatton, not being convinced beyond a reasonable doubt that he intentionally or recklessly left the stove on 'high'.
propositions.quote: In the end, he acquitted Mr. Tatton because he was not convinced beyond a reasonable doubt that Mr. Tatton intentionally or recklessly left the stove on “high”.

propositions.text: A majority of the Court of Appeal upheld the acquittal; one judge would have ordered a new trial.
propositions.quote: A majority of the Court of Appeal for Ontario upheld Mr. Tatton’s acquittal. The third member of the panel would have allowed the appeal and ordered a new trial.

paragraphs.summary: The trial judge found s. 434 to be specific intent, acquitted Mr. Tatton, and the majority of the Court of Appeal upheld the acquittal.

propositions.text: The Crown appeals, arguing arson under s. 434 is a general intent offence, so intoxication short of automatism is not a defence.
propositions.quote: The Crown appeals to this Court as of right. It argues that arson contrary to s. 434 is a general intent offence, meaning that intoxication falling short of automatism cannot be considered.

propositions.text: The court agrees arson under s. 434 is a general intent offence and a new trial is required due to the trial judge’s error.
propositions.quote: I agree. I further agree that a new trial is required because the trial judge’s critical findings of fact were tainted by his belief that self-induced intoxication was relevant to the issue of intent.

propositions.text: The appeal is allowed, the acquittal is set aside, and a new trial is ordered.
propositions.quote: Accordingly, I would allow the appeal, set aside the verdict of acquittal, and order a new trial.

paragraphs.summary: The Crown argues arson is general intent; the court agrees, finds error below, allows the appeal, and orders a new trial.

propositions.text: The only live issue at trial was whether Mr. Tatton caused the fire intentionally or recklessly.
propositions.quote: The only live issue before the trial judge was whether Mr. Tatton had caused the fire intentionally or recklessly.

propositions.text: If the fire was accidental or negligent, the required intent for conviction under s. 434 could not be inferred.
propositions.quote: On the other hand, if the fire started by reason of accident or negligence, then it could not be inferred that Mr. Tatton had one of the intents required to support a conviction under s. 434 .

paragraphs.summary: At trial, the key issue was whether Mr. Tatton acted intentionally or recklessly; accident or negligence would preclude the required intent.

propositions.text: The trial judge found Mr. Tatton was heavily intoxicated at the time of the fire.
propositions.quote: The trial judge found that Mr. Tatton was heavily under the influence of alcohol at the time of the fire.

propositions.text: The trial judge held it was necessary to determine if arson was a specific or general intent crime to decide if intoxication could be considered.
propositions.quote: Consequently, he held that it was necessary to determine whether arson was a crime of specific or general intent. The answer to that question would dictate whether Mr. Tatton’s intoxication could be considered.

paragraphs.summary: The trial judge found Mr. Tatton heavily intoxicated and needed to decide if arson was specific or general intent to assess intoxication's relevance.

propositions.text: The trial judge concluded s. 434's classification as general or specific intent was fact-driven, depending on how the fire started.
propositions.quote: The trial judge concluded that the characterization of s. 434 as either an offence of general or specific intent was fact-driven. In his view, the proper characterization depended on how the fire started.

propositions.text: If the fire was started simply, arson would likely be general intent; if more nuanced, it could be specific intent.
propositions.quote: If an accused started a fire with a match and combustible material, the charge of arson would likely be one of general intent. However, if the way in which the fire started was more nuanced, it could be a specific intent offence.

propositions.text: On these facts, the trial judge found arson was specific intent, so intoxication could be considered; he acquitted Mr. Tatton.
propositions.quote: On the facts before him, the trial judge found that the offence was one of specific intent, such that Mr. Tatton’s state of intoxication could be considered. In the end, he was not “satisfied beyond a reasonable doubt that [Mr. Tatton] left the setting [on the stove] on ‘high’ either intentionally or recklessly”: A.R., vol. I, at p. 81. Accordingly, he acquitted Mr. Tatton on the charge of arson.

paragraphs.summary: The trial judge found s. 434's classification fact-driven; here, he found it specific intent, considered intoxication, and acquitted Mr. Tatton.

propositions.text: The Court of Appeal unanimously rejected the trial judge’s fact-driven approach, holding s. 434's classification is a question of law.
propositions.quote: The Court of Appeal unanimously rejected the trial judge’s conclusion that the characterization of s. 434 as an offence of general or specific intent was fact-driven and dependent on how the fire started. Rather, the court determined — correctly in my view — that the characterization of s. 434 amounted to a question of law.

propositions.text: The Court of Appeal divided on whether s. 434 is general or specific intent.
propositions.quote: On that question, the court divided.

paragraphs.summary: The Court of Appeal held s. 434's classification is a legal question, not fact-driven, but split on whether it is general or specific intent.

propositions.text: Justice Pardu (majority) found arson under s. 434 is a specific intent offence, requiring awareness of distant consequences and a decision to proceed.
propositions.quote: Writing for the majority, Pardu J.A. characterized arson under s. 434 as a specific intent offence. In her view, s. 434 required a voluntary act, coupled with an awareness of the more distant consequences of that act, and a decision to proceed in the face of those consequences.

propositions.text: Justice Pardu noted many household activities cause fires but do not show intent or recklessness to damage property.
propositions.quote: Justice Pardu noted that many ordinary household activities cause fires; however, they do not lead inevitably to the conclusion that the person intentionally or recklessly damaged property.

propositions.text: Justice Pardu found no basis to conclude intoxication plays a significant role in causing household fires.
propositions.quote: Furthermore, there was no basis to conclude that intoxication played a significant role in causing household fires.

paragraphs.summary: Justice Pardu (majority) found s. 434 is specific intent, requiring awareness of consequences, and that intoxication is not a major cause of household fires.

propositions.text: Justice Pardu held that if arson were general intent, its mens rea would be objective, not subjective.
propositions.quote: Justice Pardu also maintained that if arson were to be characterized as a general intent offence, the mens rea for the offence would be objective, not subjective.

propositions.text: She found the words 'intentionally or recklessly' require considering the accused’s subjective state of mind, making intoxication relevant.
propositions.quote: In her view, the words “intentionally or recklessly” require consideration of an accused’s subjective state of mind, to which intoxication is relevant.

propositions.text: She concluded s. 434 is a specific intent offence and upheld Mr. Tatton’s acquittal.
propositions.quote: Consequently, she found that s. 434 was a specific intent offence, and upheld Mr. Tatton’s acquittal.

paragraphs.summary: Justice Pardu held s. 434 is specific intent, requiring subjective mens rea, so intoxication is relevant; she upheld Mr. Tatton’s acquittal.

propositions.text: Justice Goudge (dissent) concluded s. 434 is a general intent offence; intoxication short of automatism is not a defence.
propositions.quote: In dissent, Goudge J.A. concluded that s. 434 was a general intent offence and that intoxication short of automatism could therefore not be considered.

propositions.text: He held s. 434's mens rea does not extend beyond the actus reus and requires no ulterior purpose.
propositions.quote: He held that the mens rea for s. 434 did not extend beyond the actus reus, and that no ulterior purpose was required.

propositions.text: He believed arson is often committed while intoxicated, so policy reasons support barring self-induced intoxication as a defence.
propositions.quote: He was also of the view that arson is the type of offence that people are apt to commit when intoxicated; therefore, there were good policy reasons for refusing to allow an accused to raise the defence of self-induced intoxication.

paragraphs.summary: Justice Goudge (dissent) found s. 434 is general intent, with no ulterior purpose, and policy reasons support barring intoxication as a defence.

propositions.text: Justice Goudge disagreed that precluding intoxication makes mens rea objective; the inquiry remains subjective, focused on the accused’s foresight while sober.
propositions.quote: Justice Goudge disagreed with the majority that precluding reliance on intoxication transformed the mens rea inquiry into an objective one. In his view, the inquiry does not ask if a reasonable person would have foreseen the risk of damage to property; rather, one asks if the particular accused, while sober, would have foreseen the risk.

propositions.text: He concluded arson under s. 434 is not a specific intent offence and the trial judge erred in finding otherwise.
propositions.quote: It followed that arson under s. 434 was not a specific intent offence and that the trial judge erred in concluding otherwise.

propositions.text: He held the error affected the outcome and would have ordered a new trial.
propositions.quote: Justice Goudge held that the error had a material bearing on the outcome. Hence, he would have ordered a new trial.

paragraphs.summary: Justice Goudge found the inquiry remains subjective, s. 434 is not specific intent, and the trial judge's error warranted a new trial.

propositions.text: Is arson under s. 434 a general or specific intent offence?
propositions.quote: 1. Is arson contrary to s. 434 a general or specific intent offence?

propositions.text: If arson is a general intent offence, did the trial judge’s error affect the verdict?
propositions.quote: 2. If arson contrary to s. 434 is a general intent offence, did the trial judge’s error have a material bearing on the verdict?

paragraphs.summary: The court identifies two issues: the intent classification of s. 434 and whether any error affected the verdict.

propositions.text: Classifying an offence as general or specific intent affects whether self-induced intoxication short of automatism is a defence.
propositions.quote: The classification of an offence as one involving general or specific intent has important consequences for the accused. The law does not allow offenders to rely on self-induced intoxication falling short of automatism as an excuse for general intent offences: R. v. Daviault, [1994] 3 S.C.R. 63, at p. 123; R. v. Bernard, [1988] 2 S.C.R. 833, at pp. 865 and 878-80.

paragraphs.summary: The classification of an offence as general or specific intent determines if self-induced intoxication short of automatism is a defence.

propositions.text: The labels 'general intent' and 'specific intent' are not helpful in describing the mental element required for a crime.
propositions.quote: the labels “general intent” and “specific intent” are entrenched in Canadian law, they are not particularly helpful in describing the actual mental element required for a crime

propositions.text: The distinction between general and specific intent lies in the complexity of thought and reasoning processes and the social policy underlying the offence.
propositions.quote: the distinction lies in the complexity of the thought and reasoning processes that make up the mental element of a particular offence, and the social policy underlying the offence.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds that the general/specific intent distinction is unhelpful and actually depends on the complexity of mental processes and social policy.

propositions.text: Daviault is the leading case on the general/specific intent distinction but has not resolved confusion on the issue.
propositions.quote: This Court’s decision in Daviault is the leading case on the distinction between general and specific intent crimes. Unfortunately, it has not resolved the confusion surrounding this issue.

propositions.text: The general/specific intent dichotomy is criticized as illogical and leading to arbitrary and inconsistent results.
propositions.quote: It has been criticized as illogical and as leading to “arbitrary and inconsistent results from court to court, offence to offence and jurisdiction to jurisdiction”

paragraphs.summary: The court notes Daviault is the leading case but confusion and criticism about the general/specific intent distinction persist.

propositions.text: Confusion about general/specific intent is part of a larger problem in Canadian criminal law regarding unclear mental elements in the Criminal Code.
propositions.quote: The confusion surrounding the general/specific intent distinction is part of a larger problem that has plagued the Canadian criminal law for decades.

propositions.text: Judges must determine the required mental element due to lack of clear legislative direction.
propositions.quote: It is therefore left to judges to attempt to divine the required mental element (also referred to as the degree of fault).

propositions.text: Professor Don Stuart states that confusion about fault requirements undermines the legitimacy of the adversary system and presumption of innocence.
propositions.quote: Our adversary system, which requires cases to be fairly put to impartial judges or juries, and the presumption of innocence, cannot work with legitimacy where there is confusion as to the applicable tests on even basic matters such as the fault requirement . . . .

paragraphs.summary: The court and Professor Stuart note that unclear mental elements in the Criminal Code create confusion and undermine the justice system.

propositions.text: Academics and law reform bodies urge Criminal Code amendment to specify mental element and fault for each crime.
propositions.quote: He and other academics and law reform bodies have urged that the Criminal Code be amended to specify the mental element and fault requirement for each crime

paragraphs.summary: The court notes that academics and law reform bodies want the Criminal Code to specify the mental element for each crime.

propositions.text: The lack of legislative clarity causes difficulty in classifying offences as general or specific intent.
propositions.quote: The shortcoming identified by Professor Stuart and other scholars is the source of the difficulty in determining whether an offence is one of general or specific intent.

propositions.text: Legislative intervention is needed to clarify mental elements and intoxication defences, but courts must use the current regime until then.
propositions.quote: Legislative intervention is sorely needed to spell out the mental element of offences and to specify when intoxication short of automatism can be considered. However, until that day comes we are left with the existing regime.

propositions.text: The court will review Daviault's analysis before classifying the offence in s. 434 of the Criminal Code.
propositions.quote: before turning to the proper classification of the offence in s. 434 of the Criminal Code , I propose to review the analysis in Daviault

paragraphs.summary: The court finds legislative clarity is needed but will review Daviault before classifying the s. 434 offence.

propositions.text: In Daviault, the SCC examined if extreme intoxication can be a defence to a general intent crime.
propositions.quote: In Daviault, this Court examined whether an accused who is in a state of extreme intoxication, akin to automatism, may rely on drunkenness as a defence to a general intent crime.

propositions.text: Sopinka J. identified two factors distinguishing general from specific intent crimes: the nature/importance of the mental element and the social policy behind criminalizing the conduct.
propositions.quote: He held that two factors help distinguish crimes of general intent from those of specific intent: first, “[t]he nature of the mental element and its relative importance” and second, “the social policy sought to be attained by criminalizing the particular conduct”

paragraphs.summary: The court recounts that Daviault identified two factors—mental element and social policy—for distinguishing general and specific intent crimes.

propositions.text: General intent crimes involve minimal intent to do the actus reus and require little mental acuity.
propositions.quote: general intent crimes involve “the minimal intent to do the act which constitutes the actus reus”

propositions.text: High intoxication short of automatism is unlikely to negate the minimal mental element of general intent crimes.
propositions.quote: even a high degree of intoxication short of automatism is unlikely to deprive the accused of the slight degree of mental acuity required to commit them

propositions.text: For general intent crimes, intent can usually be inferred from the act, so intoxication is not a defence.
propositions.quote: one can typically infer intent from the performance of the act. It is therefore logical that for crimes involving a minimal mental element, intoxication short of automatism will have no role to play.

propositions.text: General intent crimes are often those that intoxicated persons are apt to commit, so policy precludes intoxication as a defence.
propositions.quote: general intent crimes tend to be “offences that persons who are drunk are apt to commit” (ibid.). It followed, in his view, that allowing intoxication to operate as a defence would contradict the social policy underlying these crimes.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains that general intent crimes require minimal mental acuity, so intoxication is not a defence, and policy supports this.

propositions.text: Specific intent crimes require a heightened mental element, often involving ulterior motives or purposes.
propositions.quote: specific intent crimes require a heightened mental element. For example, they often require “the formation of further ulterior motives and purposes”

propositions.text: Intoxication short of automatism may negate the mental element in specific intent crimes due to their complexity.
propositions.quote: Because such crimes require more complicated thought and reasoning processes, one can readily understand how intoxication short of automatism may negate the required mental element.

propositions.text: Specific intent offences are less likely to be committed by intoxicated people, so policy concerns are less pressing.
propositions.quote: specific intent offences are less likely to be the type of offences that intoxicated people are apt to commit. For that reason, policy considerations that might otherwise militate against a defence of intoxication are less pressing.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains that specific intent crimes require complex reasoning, so intoxication may negate intent and policy concerns are less significant.

propositions.text: Another policy reason for allowing intoxication as a defence to specific intent offences is that they often include lesser general intent offences, so punishment is not avoided.
propositions.quote: specific intent offences often include lesser offences that only require general intent. In such cases, an intoxicated offender will not escape punishment altogether

paragraphs.summary: The court notes that specific intent offences often include lesser general intent offences, so intoxication as a defence does not mean escaping punishment.

propositions.text: Classifying an offence as specific or general intent starts with determining its mental element through statutory interpretation, not factual assessment.
propositions.quote: The analysis of whether an offence is one of specific or general intent must start with a determination of the mental element of the offence in question. This is an exercise in statutory interpretation. Care should be taken not to turn it into a factual assessment based on the circumstances of the particular case.

paragraphs.summary: The court states that classifying intent requires statutory interpretation of the offence's mental element, not a factual case-by-case assessment.

propositions.text: After determining the mental element, the next step is to decide if the crime is general or specific intent, which involves logic, intuition, and policy.
propositions.quote: After the mental element of the provision has been determined, the next question is whether the crime is one of general or specific intent. The distinction between general and specific intent offences is not a precise science. Logic, intuition, and policy all play a part.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains that deciding between general and specific intent involves logic, intuition, and policy after determining the mental element.

propositions.text: Courts should look to existing jurisprudence to classify offences; if unclear, they must use Daviault's factors.
propositions.quote: the place to begin in determining the appropriate classification of the offence is to look to existing jurisprudence. Where the jurisprudence has already determined the appropriate classification of the offence in a satisfactory manner, the task is straightforward... However, if the jurisprudence is unclear, courts must examine the factors outlined in Daviault, as clarified below, to resolve the question.

paragraphs.summary: The court says to use existing case law to classify offences, but if unclear, apply Daviault's factors.

propositions.text: Daviault identified two main considerations: the 'importance' of the mental element and the social policy underlying the offence.
propositions.quote: Daviault made clear that there are two main considerations when determining if intoxication short of automatism can be considered — the “importance” of the mental element, and the social policy underlying the offence

propositions.text: Daviault did not clarify what 'importance' of the mental element means or when policy should be considered.
propositions.quote: it provided no clear explanation of what is meant by the “importance” of the mental element. Second, it did not specify whether policy considerations should always play a role in the analysis or whether they should only come into play if an examination of the mental element left unclear how the offence should be characterized.

propositions.text: The court will address these questions to clarify the law.
propositions.quote: I turn to these questions in the hope of bringing some added clarity to an area of the law that continues to perplex and confound.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes Daviault left questions about the 'importance' of the mental element and policy's role, which it now seeks to clarify.

propositions.text: 'Importance' of the mental element refers to the complexity of thought and reasoning required for the offence.
propositions.quote: it is clear that he was referring to the complexity of the thought and reasoning processes that make up the mental element of a particular offence.

propositions.text: General intent crimes require straightforward thought and reasoning; specific intent crimes require more sophisticated reasoning.
propositions.quote: The thought and reasoning processes for general intent crimes are relatively straightforward. In contrast, specific intent crimes — those crimes with a more “important” mental element — require a more sophisticated reasoning process.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds that 'importance' means complexity of reasoning, with general intent being straightforward and specific intent requiring sophistication.

propositions.text: General intent crimes require intent to perform the illegal act, not to bring about external consequences or complex knowledge.
propositions.quote: For general intent crimes, the mental element simply relates to the performance of an illegal act. Such crimes do not require an intent to bring about certain consequences that are external to the actus reus

propositions.text: General intent crimes do not require actual knowledge of circumstances or consequences if such knowledge involves complex reasoning.
propositions.quote: crimes of general intent do not require actual knowledge of certain circumstances or consequences, to the extent that such knowledge is the product of complex thought and reasoning processes.

propositions.text: The mental element for general intent crimes is straightforward and requires little mental acuity.
propositions.quote: In each instance, the mental element is straightforward and requires little mental acuity.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains that general intent crimes require only intent to act, not complex knowledge or intent to cause consequences.

propositions.text: 'Straightforward' and 'little mental acuity' are synonymous with Daviault's 'minimal intent' and 'minimal degree of consciousness.'
propositions.quote: I am using these phrases synonymously with the descriptors used in Daviault: “minimal intent” and “minimal degree of consciousness”

paragraphs.summary: The court clarifies that 'straightforward' and 'little mental acuity' mean the same as Daviault's 'minimal intent.'

propositions.text: Specific intent offences involve a heightened mental element, often requiring an ulterior purpose beyond the actus reus.
propositions.quote: specific intent offences involve a heightened mental element. In Daviault, Sopinka J. limited his discussion of specific intent offences to crimes involving an ulterior purpose.

propositions.text: For such crimes, the accused must intend the act and act with an ulterior purpose, regardless of success.
propositions.quote: The accused must not only commit the assault, he must also act with the ulterior purpose of resisting arrest. It is irrelevant whether he actually succeeds in resisting arrest; the offence simply requires that he act with that purpose in mind.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains that specific intent offences require intent to act and an ulterior purpose, regardless of whether the purpose is achieved.

propositions.text: An ulterior purpose is not always required for specific intent; a heightened mental element can also be intent to bring about consequences or actual knowledge involving complex reasoning.
propositions.quote: it would be a mistake to assume that an ulterior purpose is always required. To the contrary, a heightened mental element could take the form of a requirement that the accused intend and bring about certain consequences, if the formation of that intent involves more complex thought and reasoning processes.

propositions.text: Murder and possession of stolen property are examples of specific intent crimes due to their complex mental elements.
propositions.quote: Murder provides a classic example. Equally, a heightened mental element could take the form of a requirement that the accused have actual knowledge of certain circumstances or consequences, where the knowledge is the product of more complex thought and reasoning processes: see, e.g., M. T. Thornton, “Making Sense of Majewski” (1981), 23 Crim. L.Q. 464, at p. 482. Possession of stolen property is one such crime.

propositions.text: Intoxication is available as a defence for such crimes with heightened mental elements.
propositions.quote: Intoxication is therefore available as a defence for such crimes.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds that specific intent can involve ulterior purpose, intent to cause consequences, or complex knowledge, making intoxication a possible defence.

propositions.text: Specific intent offences have a heightened mental element, which may be ulterior purpose, complex knowledge, or intent to cause consequences; general intent requires little mental acuity.
propositions.quote: specific intent offences contain a heightened mental element. That element may take the form of an ulterior purpose or it may entail actual knowledge of certain circumstances or consequences, where the knowledge is the product of more complex thought and reasoning processes. Alternatively, it may involve intent to bring about certain consequences, if the formation of that intent involves more complex thought and reasoning processes. General intent offences, on the other hand, require very little mental acuity.

paragraphs.summary: The court summarizes that specific intent involves heightened mental elements, while general intent requires little mental acuity.

propositions.text: Daviault left unclear whether policy should always be considered or only when the mental element is unclear.
propositions.quote: Confusion remains about whether policy should be considered in every case or whether it should only come into play if an examination of the mental element leaves it unclear how the offence should be characterized.

paragraphs.summary: The court identifies the unresolved issue of when policy should be considered in classifying offences as general or specific intent.

propositions.text: The most logical approach is to first examine the nature of the mental element before considering policy.
propositions.quote: the most logical approach is to first examine the nature of the mental element. Only when this analysis fails to yield a clear answer should one turn to policy considerations.

propositions.text: Policy considerations are closely tied to the nature of the mental element in intent crimes.
propositions.quote: policy considerations are closely tied to the nature of the mental element.

propositions.text: General intent crimes require minimal mental acuity, so intoxication short of automatism rarely negates intent.
propositions.quote: General intent crimes involve such minimal mental acuity that it is difficult to see how intoxication short of automatism could deprive the accused of the low level of intent required.

propositions.text: Policy supports precluding intoxication as a defence for general intent offences, and this is constitutionally permissible.
propositions.quote: This provides a strong policy reason for precluding reliance on intoxication for these offences: Daviault, at p. 123. It also explains why it is constitutionally permissible to render the intoxication defence unavailable for general intent offences: ibid., at pp. 99-100.

propositions.text: Specific intent crimes require more complex reasoning, so intoxication may negate intent and policy supports allowing the defence.
propositions.quote: one can more readily understand how the more complex thought and reasoning processes required for specific intent crimes may be negated by an accused’s intoxication. For that reason, policy suggests that intoxication can be considered for specific intent crimes.

propositions.text: If the mental element analysis clearly indicates the offence's characterization, policy considerations are unnecessary.
propositions.quote: if an examination of the mental element clearly indicates how the offence should be characterized, there is little reason to resort to policy considerations.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains that the nature of the mental element should be examined first, with policy considerations secondary, especially regarding intoxication and intent.

propositions.text: If the mental element analysis is unclear, policy considerations may help resolve the issue.
propositions.quote: if an examination of the mental element does not provide a clear answer, policy considerations may help resolve the question.

propositions.text: Policy focuses on whether alcohol is habitually associated with the crime; if so, allowing intoxication as a defence is counterintuitive.
propositions.quote: the policy assessment will focus on whether alcohol consumption is habitually associated with the crime in question. If it is, then allowing an accused to rely on intoxication as a defence would seem counterintuitive.

propositions.text: For crimes rarely associated with intoxication, preventing the defence makes less sense from a policy perspective.
propositions.quote: where self-induced intoxication rarely, if ever, plays a role in the commission of a particular crime, preventing an accused from relying on it makes less sense from a policy perspective.

paragraphs.summary: The court states that if the mental element is unclear, policy—especially the association of alcohol with the crime—may guide whether intoxication is a defence.

propositions.text: Alcohol is often involved in violent or unruly crimes and property damage, so policy disfavors intoxication as a defence for these.
propositions.quote: alcohol habitually plays a role in crimes involving violent or unruly conduct: Bernard, at p. 880. It also tends to be prevalent in crimes involving damage to property. As such, it makes little sense from a policy perspective that it should provide a defence for crimes in which people or property are harmed or endangered: Daviault, at p. 123.

propositions.text: There are exceptions, such as murder, where intoxication is a defence due to the offence's complexity and gravity.
propositions.quote: Murder, for example, has long been considered a crime of specific intent for which the defence of intoxication is available.

propositions.text: It is incorrect to say intoxication is never a defence for crimes involving violence or property damage, but policy usually weighs against it.
propositions.quote: it is incorrect to state that intoxication may never be considered in crimes involving violence against people or damage to property. However, given the prevalence of alcohol in these crimes, there are likely to be strong policy reasons militating against an intoxication-based defence.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds alcohol is common in violent/property crimes, so policy disfavors intoxication as a defence, with exceptions like murder.

propositions.text: Other policy considerations, like the presence of a lesser included general intent offence, may be relevant.
propositions.quote: there are other residual policy considerations that may also come into play. As noted in Daviault, the presence of a lesser included general intent offence in the main offence may be relevant.

propositions.text: If a lesser included offence exists, an accused may still be convicted of it even if intoxication negates the main offence's intent.
propositions.quote: an accused who successfully relies on intoxication to negate the heightened mental element of the main offence can still be convicted of the lesser included offence.

propositions.text: In such cases, the intoxicated offender will not escape punishment, reducing the need to preclude the intoxication defence for the main offence.
propositions.quote: the intoxicated offender will not escape punishment altogether. Consequently, there is less impetus to preclude the accused from advancing intoxication as a defence to the main offence.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes that if a lesser included offence exists, policy concerns about intoxication as a defence are lessened since punishment remains possible.

propositions.text: Judicial sentencing discretion is a factor; if a heavy minimum sentence applies, precluding intoxication as a defence may be harsh.
propositions.quote: If the crime is one for which the accused will receive a heavy minimum sentence upon conviction, it may be unduly harsh to preclude consideration of intoxication.

propositions.text: If the judge has sentencing discretion, precluding the intoxication defence is less concerning.
propositions.quote: if the judge has discretion to tailor the sentence to the facts of the case and to consider the accused’s intoxication as part of that assessment, precluding the accused from advancing a defence of intoxication is less worrisome: Daviault, at p. 124.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds that sentencing discretion affects whether precluding intoxication as a defence is harsh or less concerning.

propositions.text: Arson's classification as general or specific intent has divided courts historically.
propositions.quote: Over the years, courts have been divided on whether the offence of arson in s. 434 (and its predecessors) is a crime of general or specific intent

paragraphs.summary: The court notes that courts have historically disagreed on whether arson under s. 434 is a general or specific intent offence.

propositions.text: Section 434 arson is a general intent offence; intoxication short of automatism is not a defence.
propositions.quote: I am satisfied that s. 434 is a general intent offence for which intoxication falling short of automatism is not available as a defence.

propositions.text: Section 434 criminalizes intentionally or recklessly causing damage by fire or explosion to property not wholly owned by the accused.
propositions.quote: 434. Every person who intentionally or recklessly causes damage by fire or explosion to property that is not wholly owned by that person is guilty of an indictable offence and liable to imprisonment for a term not exceeding fourteen years.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds s. 434 arson is a general intent offence, so intoxication short of automatism is not a defence.

propositions.text: The actus reus is damaging property by fire; the mental element is intentional or reckless causation of damage, requiring minimal intent.
propositions.quote: The actus reus is the damaging of property by fire. The mental element is the intentional or reckless performance of the illegal act — the causing of damage to property. No additional knowledge or purpose is needed. No complex thought or reasoning processes are required. On its face, the level of intent required for the offence would appear to be minimal.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds s. 434 requires only minimal intent: intentionally or recklessly causing property damage by fire.

propositions.text: The Court of Appeal majority worried that classifying s. 434 as general intent would make recklessness objective, but the court disagrees.
propositions.quote: A majority of the Court of Appeal was concerned that if s. 434 were found to be a general intent offence, so as to preclude consideration of intoxication short of automatism, that would improperly transform the examination of recklessness into an objective inquiry. With respect, I cannot agree.

propositions.text: Recklessness is always a subjective inquiry, including for s. 434 arson.
propositions.quote: Recklessness describes the act of one who sees the risk and acts without regard for the consequences: Sansregret v. The Queen, [1985] 1 S.C.R. 570, at p. 582. It always involves a subjective inquiry — and this case is no exception.

propositions.text: Arson under s. 434 does not require sophisticated reasoning; the risk of fire damage is typically obvious.
propositions.quote: the offence of arson under s. 434 does not involve sophisticated reasoning. The risk of damage by fire is typically obvious, even when it involves a chain of events and not the simple application of a match to the property in question.

paragraphs.summary: The court disagrees with the Court of Appeal, finding recklessness under s. 434 remains subjective and does not require complex reasoning.

propositions.text: Intoxication short of automatism is unlikely to prevent foreseeing fire damage; minimal intent suffices for s. 434.
propositions.quote: I have difficulty seeing how intoxication short of automatism would prevent an accused from foreseeing the risk of causing damage to someone else’s property by fire. Complex reasoning is not required to recognize the danger.

propositions.text: Preventing the intoxication defence does not make recklessness objective, but reflects that minimal intent is not negated by intoxication.
propositions.quote: Thus, preventing an accused from advancing the defence of intoxication does not transform recklessness into an objective inquiry. Rather, it recognizes the fact that intoxication short of automatism will not deprive an accused of the minimal intent required for this crime.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds intoxication short of automatism does not negate the minimal intent for s. 434, so barring the defence is appropriate.

propositions.text: Given the conclusion on intent, policy considerations are unnecessary, but would lead to the same result.
propositions.quote: there is no need to resort to policy considerations to determine the availability of the defence of intoxication. However, had I found it necessary to do so, I would have reached the same conclusion.

paragraphs.summary: The court states that policy considerations are unnecessary but would not change the result regarding intoxication and s. 434.

propositions.text: Section 434 involves property damage, often associated with alcohol; allowing intoxication as a defence would erode the offence's policy.
propositions.quote: Section 434 involves damage to property. Damage to property is often associated with alcohol consumption. The present case is no exception. In my view, it would erode the policy underlying the offence of causing damage to property by fire if an accused could rely on self-induced intoxication as a defence.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds that allowing intoxication as a defence for s. 434 would undermine the policy against property damage by fire.

propositions.text: The trial judge and Court of Appeal majority erred in treating s. 434 as specific intent; it is general intent, so intoxication is not a defence.
propositions.quote: the trial judge and the majority of the Court of Appeal erred in characterizing s. 434 as a specific intent offence for which the defence of intoxication could be raised. Properly classified, s. 434 is a general intent offence, meaning that intoxication short of automatism may not be considered.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the lower courts erred; s. 434 is general intent, so intoxication short of automatism is not a defence.

propositions.text: Determining intent under s. 434 can be complex due to varied factual scenarios; the court offers guidance for triers of fact.
propositions.quote: ascertaining whether the intent required under s. 434 has been made out in a particular case can be a tricky exercise.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes that intent under s. 434 can be complex and offers suggestions for fact-finders.

propositions.text: The criminal act in s. 434 is causing property damage, not merely setting a fire; this distinction is crucial.
propositions.quote: The conduct that has been criminalized is the causing of damage to property. The fire is simply the mechanism by which the damage must be caused. This distinction is crucial to the analysis.

paragraphs.summary: The court clarifies that s. 434 criminalizes causing property damage, not just setting a fire.

propositions.text: All surrounding circumstances, including how the fire started, are relevant to intent, but are not dispositive for s. 434.
propositions.quote: the trier of fact must of course consider all of the surrounding circumstances. How the fire started is likely to be an important consideration. Specifically, was the fire set accidentally, negligently, recklessly, or intentionally? The answer to this question will not be dispositive since, as I have explained, the act of setting a fire is not the conduct that has been criminalized under s. 434 . Nonetheless, it will provide important context for the intent analysis.

paragraphs.summary: The court states that how the fire started is important context but not determinative for intent under s. 434.

propositions.text: Intent under s. 434 depends on all circumstances; intentional or reckless fire-setting may not suffice without context showing intent to damage property.
propositions.quote: The end game involves looking at all of the surrounding circumstances to determine whether it can be inferred that the accused intended to cause damage to someone else’s property or was reckless whether damage ensued or not. The mere fact that the fire was set intentionally or recklessly may not be enough to establish that the accused intentionally or recklessly caused damage to the property. Context is important and will play a key role in determining whether such an inference can be drawn.

propositions.text: Example: a controlled fire spreading accidentally does not necessarily show intent or recklessness regarding property damage.
propositions.quote: If a gust of wind picks up some burning leaves from the fire pit and blows them onto a neighbour’s shed 20 metres away, it does not follow that he intentionally or recklessly damaged the shed.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds that intent under s. 434 requires context; intentional fire-setting alone may not prove intent to damage property.

propositions.text: In some cases, circumstances make clear the accused intended or was reckless about property damage, e.g., setting a towel on fire and leaving it.
propositions.quote: If that person were to drop the towel on the carpet and walk away without making any effort to extinguish the fire, it may be inferred that he or she intended to cause damage to property or was reckless whether damage ensued.

paragraphs.summary: The court gives an example where intent or recklessness regarding property damage is clear from the circumstances.

propositions.text: The key question is whether the accused intentionally or recklessly caused property damage, not merely how the fire started.
propositions.quote: An accused’s guilt under s. 434 hinges on whether he or she intentionally or recklessly caused damage to the property in question.

propositions.text: Triers of fact should focus on context and circumstances to analyze intent under s. 434.
propositions.quote: So long as the trier of fact keeps this important distinction in mind and examines the relevant context and surrounding circumstances, the analysis of intent under s. 434 should be relatively straightforward.

paragraphs.summary: The court emphasizes that guilt under s. 434 depends on intent or recklessness regarding property damage, considering all circumstances.

propositions.text: Whether the trial judge’s error regarding intoxication had a material bearing on the acquittal, affecting the Crown's entitlement to a new trial.
propositions.quote: To obtain a new trial, the Crown must demonstrate that the error might reasonably have had a material bearing on the acquittal.

propositions.text: The Crown must show the error might reasonably have affected the acquittal, not just a hypothetical possibility.
propositions.quote: It has been long established, however, that an appeal by the Attorney General cannot succeed on an abstract or purely hypothetical possibility that the accused would have been convicted but for the error of law. Something more must be shown.

propositions.text: The Crown need not prove the verdict would necessarily have been different, only that the error might reasonably have had a material bearing.
propositions.quote: The Attorney General is not required, however, to persuade us that the verdict would necessarily have been different.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the Crown must show the trial judge's error might reasonably have affected the acquittal to obtain a new trial.

propositions.text: The trial judge based the acquittal on the defence of accident and intoxication was irrelevant.
propositions.quote: Mr. Tatton submits that the trial judge based the acquittal on the defence of accident and that intoxication had no bearing on the analysis.

propositions.text: The trial judge’s error could not have affected the verdict.
propositions.quote: he therefore argues that the trial judge’s error cannot reasonably be thought to have affected the verdict.

propositions.text: The trial judge’s reasons show he considered Mr. Tatton’s intoxication in reaching the verdict.
propositions.quote: The Crown, on the other hand, argues that the trial judge’s reasons make it clear that he considered Mr. Tatton’s intoxication in arriving at the verdict.

paragraphs.summary: Mr. Tatton argues the acquittal was based on accident, not intoxication, while the Crown says intoxication was considered by the trial judge.

propositions.text: The Crown’s submission is accepted; the trial judge’s reasons show intoxication played a material role in the outcome.
propositions.quote: I accept the Crown’s submission. In my view, when the trial judge’s reasons are read in their entirety, it is apparent that Mr. Tatton’s intoxication played a material role in the outcome.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds that the trial judge's reasons show intoxication was material to the outcome, agreeing with the Crown.

propositions.text: The trial judge focused on the cause of the fire and whether Tatton intentionally or recklessly started it.
propositions.quote: In his reasons, the trial judge concentrated on the cause of the fire. In particular, the question he posed was whether he could be satisfied that Mr. Tatton intentionally or recklessly started the fire in the frying pan.

propositions.text: The trial judge stated he must determine if Tatton’s intoxication could be considered to resolve the issue.
propositions.quote: At the outset of his analysis, the trial judge stated that to resolve this issue, he must determine whether Mr. Tatton’s intoxication could be considered.

propositions.text: The trial judge’s reasons focus almost exclusively on intoxication’s role.
propositions.quote: The trial judge’s reasons focus almost exclusively on this issue.

propositions.text: If the acquittal was based on accident alone, the intoxication analysis was unnecessary.
propositions.quote: If, as Mr. Tatton argues, the trial judge concluded that the fire was accidental — separate and apart from any role alcohol may have played — all of this analysis was unnecessary.

propositions.text: It is illogical to suggest the acquittal was not influenced by the trial judge’s erroneous belief about considering intoxication.
propositions.quote: In my view, it defies logic and common sense to suggest that the trial judge’s decision to acquit was not influenced by his erroneous belief that he could take into account Mr. Tatton’s state of intoxication.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the trial judge focused on intoxication, making it illogical to say the acquittal was based solely on accident.

propositions.text: The trial judge’s concluding remarks show intoxication was a key concern in finding reasonable doubt.
propositions.quote: In finding that he was left in a state of reasonable doubt, the trial judge stated that one of the questions troubling him was whether Mr. Tatton was “mentally able to carry out such a plan, in view of his drunken condition”

propositions.text: Tatton’s inebriation was at the forefront of the trial judge’s mind.
propositions.quote: Plainly, Mr. Tatton’s inebriation was at the forefront of the trial judge’s mind.

propositions.text: The trial judge noted Tatton’s position that the fire was accidental but did not explicitly find accident.
propositions.quote: Although the trial judge noted Mr. Tatton’s position that the fire was accidental, he did not explicitly make a finding of accident.

propositions.text: The trial judge was not satisfied beyond a reasonable doubt that Tatton acted intentionally or recklessly.
propositions.quote: Rather, he stated that he was not satisfied beyond a reasonable doubt that Mr. Tatton had acted intentionally or recklessly.

propositions.text: The clear implication is that intoxication left the trial judge in doubt about intent, meeting the Graveline test.
propositions.quote: the clear implication from his reasons is that it was Mr. Tatton’s state of intoxication that left him in a state of reasonable doubt as to whether Mr. Tatton acted with the requisite intent. That being so, I am satisfied that the test in Graveline has been met.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the trial judge's doubt was due to intoxication, not accident, thus meeting the Graveline test for appellate intervention.

propositions.text: The appeal is allowed, the acquittal is set aside, and a new trial is ordered.
propositions.quote: For these reasons, I would allow the appeal, set aside the acquittal, and order a new trial. Appeal allowed.

paragraphs.summary: The court allows the appeal, sets aside the acquittal, and orders a new trial.
